title: What does the MAS stablecoin framework require, and how quickly must an issuer redeem at par?
abstract: Sourced guide to the Monetary Authority of Singapore's stablecoin framework: which stablecoins it covers, reserve and capital rules, redemption timing and disclosure.
body:
According to the Monetary Authority of Singapore, its stablecoin framework covers single-currency stablecoins pegged to the Singapore dollar or a G10 currency and issued in Singapore. Issuers must return par value within five business days of a redemption request. [1]

Reserve assets must meet requirements for composition, valuation, custody and audit, to give a high degree of assurance of value stability. Issuers must hold minimum base capital and liquid assets, to reduce insolvency risk and allow an orderly wind-down. [1]

Issuers must give users disclosures that include the stablecoin's value-stabilising mechanism, holders' rights and the audit results of the reserve assets. According to MAS's Payment Services Act FAQ of April 2024, an issuer that meets every requirement can apply for its stablecoin to be recognised and labelled a MAS-regulated stablecoin, and MAS was then working on the legislative amendments needed to implement the framework. [1][2]

Author interpretation: the framework as described attaches to stablecoins issued in Singapore. A dollar stablecoin issued elsewhere, such as RLUSD, is outside that description, although the same FAQ says a stablecoin may still count as a digital payment token under the Payment Services Act. Sources accessed 11 November 2026. [1][2]
